prompt: What happens to twin-width under complementation of a finite simple graph $G$?

answers.text: $\operatorname{tww}(\overline G)=\operatorname{tww}(G)$: the same partition sequence has the same red graphs.
answers.explanation: Complementation swaps complete and empty pairs of parts, while mixed pairs remain mixed. Thus every sequence keeps exactly the same red degrees.
Complementing twice would increase the value by two while returning to the original graph.
A clique and an edgeless graph both have twin-width zero, refuting this formula.
Complementation is an involution, so this would incorrectly give twin-width zero to every graph.

answers.text: A red pair becomes black because a mixed adjacency relation becomes complete.
answers.explanation: Complementing a mixture of edges and non-edges leaves another mixture, not a complete relation.

answers.text: Every black pair becomes red because all its adjacencies change.
answers.explanation: Changing a complete pair to an empty pair preserves homogeneity; it creates no red edge.

answers.text: Every non-edge pair becomes red because new edges are introduced.
answers.explanation: An empty pair becomes complete and remains homogeneous.

answers.text: Equality is guaranteed only for graphs of bounded maximum degree.
answers.explanation: The homogeneity argument applies to every finite simple graph, irrespective of degree.

answers.text: Equality requires a different contraction sequence and fails for the original optimal sequence.
answers.explanation: The same sequence preserves exactly which pairs of parts are mixed.

answers.text: Complementation preserves only the total red-edge count; individual red degrees can change along the same partition sequence.
answers.explanation: The whole red graph is unchanged at each partition, so every individual red degree is unchanged too.
